newsitem.title: UK: PRESS DIGEST - Financial Times - Jan 13.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - Financial Times - Jan 13.

text.p: Prepared for Reuters by The Broadcast Monitoring Company -- OECD TASK FORCE SEEKS TO CURB TAX COMPETITION

The Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD), the club of advanced industrial nations, has set up a task force to investigate tax competition among countries amid fears that government revenues are being undermined and foreign investment distorted. The project has been given priority funding, and is due to be completed by May 1998. Its remit is thought to include non-OECD member countries, including traditional tax havens such as the Cayman Islands.
-- GEC-ALSTHOM PENALISED FOR LATE DELIVERY OF TRAINS

London Transport has charged a late delivery penalty to GEC- Alsthom for a 12-month delay in delivering the first in a batch of new trains. The trains are part of a contract worth between 800 million stg and 900 million stg, which the Anglo- French railway engineering group won in the face of competition from Adtranz (ABB Daimler-Benz). Adtranz was forced to make 600 staff redundant at its Derby plant after losing the bidding.
-- LABOUR DISMISSES WINDFALL TAX LEGAL CHALLENGE

A legal opinion commissioned by a Conservative think-tank has claimed that the Labour party's proposed 'windfall tax' on the privatised utilities raises 'serious legal issues', and that it could face legal challenges 'based on respectable grounds'. The advice, prepared by Gerald Barling, also suggests that even if the challenges were not successful, they could delay payment of the levy sufficiently as to raise questions over Labour's ability to fund the programmes for which the money has been earmarked. Labour has dismissed the claims as Conservative propaganda.
-- INFORMATION AGE COULD CURB INFLATION

A leading economist in the City of London has predicted that global inflation will be held in check well into the next millennium as the spread of information technology leads to worldwide price competition. The vision comes in a paper entitled 'Implications of the Information Age', prepared by David Owen, economist at Dresdner Kleinwort Benson, which also claims that information technology will exacerbate the polarisation between rich and poor countries.
-- FORD MAY CLOSE ESCORT PLANT

Ford managers at the company's Halewood plant in Merseyside are due to meet union leaders this week amid reports that the company is considering closing the plant. Ford is currently undergoing a review of its European operations following losses of 279.2 million stg in the third quarter of 1996. Halewood, which manufacturers Escorts, is seen as a possible target for closure, although the company has dismissed the reports as speculation.
-- DEMAND FOR TEMPORARY STAFF AT RECORD LEVELS

A report by recruitment group Reed Personnel Services shows that demand for temporary staff reached record levels in the final quarter of 1996. The report also reveals that over the same period demand for permanent staff fell, the first such drop for two years. Separately, the Labour party announced that figures taken from the government's Labour Force Survey show that more men were being made redundant last spring than a year earlier.
-- BRITISH GAS SEEKS GLOBAL DEAL FOR FIELDS

British Gas is looking to solve its problem with so- called 'take or pay' contracts with North Sea gas producers in one go, using its Morecambe gas fields for a 'global settlement'. The Morecambe field, off the northwest coast of England, is the main asset of Centrica, the domestic gas supply business due to be demerged in February. British Gas wants to use the field, valued at about 1.45 billion stg, in a one-off deal to release the company from onerous contracts which commit British Gas to buying gas it no longer needs at prices well above current market value.
-- SEARS TO EXPLAIN SHOCK PROFITS WARNING

Retailing group Sears is to meet its largest shareholders this week to explain the shock profits warning it announced last week, and in a bid to set out the case for retaining embattled chief executive Liam Strong. Sears said last week that group profits were unlikely to meet market expectations of about 100 million stg. The group is also expected this week to make a statement about the future of its British Shoe Corp.
-- AMP PLANS TO BUY BRITISH LIFE AND PENSIONS GROUP

Australian life assurer AMP is reported to be keen to acquire a "sizeable" British life and pensions company. The acquisition would be part of AMP's plans to double in size in Britain in the next five years. The group, Australia's largest life assurer, has said Britain would be used as a platform to expand into Europe. AMP already owns Pearl Assurance, London Life AMP Asset Management and a 50 percent stake in Virgin Direct.
-- CALENERGY TO EXPAND FROM NEWCASTLE

CalEnergy, the aggressive U.S. independent power producer which last year gained control of British regional electricity company Northern Electric with a 782 million stg hostile bid, is to use Northern's base in Newcastle as its headquarters for efforts to break into electricity supply and distribution in Europe and Asia. CalEnergy has said it also plans to enter the domestic gas and electricity supply markets when they are fully deregulated in 1998.
